segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he began to speak to them in parables:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “A man planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a pit for the winepress, and built a tower. Then he leased it to tenants and went abroad.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When the season came, he sent a slave to the tenants to collect from the tenants a share of the vineyard’s fruit.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But they seized him, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Again he sent another slave to them; that one they struck on the head and treated shamefully.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He sent yet another, and that one they killed; and so with many others, beating some and killing others.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He had one left, a beloved son. Last of all he sent him to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But those tenants said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So they seized him and killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Have you not even read this scripture: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: this came from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were looking for a way to arrest him, but they were afraid of the crowd, for they knew that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they sent some of the Pharisees and the Herodians to him, to trap him in what he said.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came and said to him,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and are swayed by no one, for you pay no regard to people’s standing but teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to give the poll tax to Caesar, or not? Should we give it, or should we not?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he, knowing their hypocrisy, said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you testing me? Bring me a denarius so that I may look at it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They brought one, and he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Whose image is this, and whose inscription?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “Caesar’s.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they were utterly amazed at him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to him and questioned him, saying,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves behind a wife but leaves no child, his brother is to take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother.

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: There were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and when he died he left no offspring.

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: The second took her and died, leaving no offspring behind, and the third likewise.

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: None of the seven left offspring. Last of all, the woman also died.

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: In the resurrection, when they rise, whose wife will she be? For all seven had her as wife.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Is this not why you are mistaken, that you know neither the scriptures nor the power of God?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God said to him, ‘I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He is not God of the dead but of the living. You are badly mistaken.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of the scribes came up and heard them debating. Seeing that Jesus had answered them well, he asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Which commandment is first of all?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The first is, ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The second is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The scribe said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Well said, Teacher. In truth you have said that he is one, and there is no other besides him;

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and to love him with all one’s heart and all one’s understanding and all one’s strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, is far more than all the whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus, seeing that he had answered thoughtfully, said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You are not far from the kingdom of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And after that no one dared to question him any longer.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As Jesus was teaching in the temple, he spoke up and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How can the scribes say that the Messiah is David’s son?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: David himself said by the Holy Spirit, ‘The Lord said to my lord, “Sit at my right hand until I put your enemies under your feet.”’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: David himself calls him lord, so how can he be his son?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the large crowd listened to him gladly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In his teaching he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Watch out for the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and to be greeted in the marketplaces,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and to have the front seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at banquets.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: They devour widows’ houses and, for show, pray at length. These will receive a harsher judgment.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He sat down opposite the treasury and watched how the crowd was putting money into the treasury. Many rich people were putting in large amounts.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then one poor widow came and put in two tiny copper coins, which make a penny.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He called his disciples to him and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all the others who are putting money into the treasury.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For they all put in out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty put in everything she had, all she had to live on.”

notes.note: The fence, the winepress pit and the tower echo the song of the vineyard in Isaiah 5:1–2, where the vineyard is Israel and its owner is God. A hearer who knew the Scriptures would catch the allusion and expect a story about God and his people. Leasing an estate to tenants for a share of the crop while the owner lived elsewhere was a familiar arrangement.

The Greek word means a person owned by another, and the first hearers understood it that way. “Servant” softens this and blurs the difference from other Greek words for attendants and helpers. Several modern translations now use “slave”; others keep “servant” to avoid association with race-based chattel slavery.

The Greek verb is extremely rare, and its meaning is inferred from its connection with the word for “head” and from the context. Most translators take it as striking or wounding the head. The exact sense remains uncertain.

The quotation is Psalm 118:22–23 in the wording of the Greek Old Testament. The phrase is literally “head of the corner.” It may mean the foundation stone at a building’s corner or the capstone that completes the top of a wall or arch, and scholars are divided. On either reading the rejected stone ends up in the most important position.

The Greek borrows the Latin word census. It refers to the head tax Rome levied on a subject population on the basis of a registration, as distinct from tolls and customs. Judea had paid it since coming under direct Roman rule, and it was resented as a mark of subjection. That is why the question is a trap: a yes would alienate the crowd, and a no could be reported as sedition.

A Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s wage for a labourer. The denarius of the reigning emperor Tiberius carried his portrait and an inscription naming him son of the divine Augustus. Many interpreters hear in the word “image” an allusion to human beings as made in God’s image, so that what is owed to God is oneself; the text does not say this outright.

The questioners asked whether to “give” the tax. Jesus answers with a compound of the same verb that means to give back or to pay what is owed. “Render” once carried this sense but no longer does in ordinary English, and “give back” keeps the echo of the question.

The reference is to Deuteronomy 25:5–6. When a married man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow, and the first son would carry on the dead man’s name. The Sadducees use this law to make resurrection look absurd, and Jesus answers them from the books of Moses, the authority they themselves appeal to.

The Greek is plural, reflecting a Hebrew and Aramaic way of speaking about God’s dwelling. Most translations flatten it to “heaven.” The plural is kept here because a first-century hearer would have noticed the Semitic turn of phrase.

notes.phrase: in the passage about the bush
notes.note: The Greek says simply “at the bush.” Before chapter and verse numbers existed, a passage was cited by a key word or subject. The reference is to the burning bush episode, and the words quoted are from Exodus 3:6. Older versions took the phrase as the place where God spoke; most modern translations take it as a citation, as here.

notes.phrase: the Lord our God, the Lord is one
notes.traditional: The Lord our God is one Lord
notes.note: This is Deuteronomy 6:4, the opening of the Shema, which devout Jews recited daily. The Greek, like the Hebrew behind it, has no verb in the first half and can be construed several ways, including “the Lord our God is one Lord” and “the Lord is our God, the Lord alone.” The scribe’s reply in verse 32, “he is one,” suggests the statement was heard as affirming God’s oneness.

Here the Greek word is a title under discussion: the anointed king Israel expected. It is not a name for Jesus. “Messiah” conveys the title to a modern reader, while “Christ” is kept where the word functions as a name. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

The quotation is Psalm 110:1. In Hebrew the first “Lord” is the divine name and the second is an ordinary word for a master or superior, while the Greek uses the same word for both. The argument assumes David is the speaker: if David calls the Messiah his superior, “son of David” cannot be the whole truth about him. Most translations capitalise both; the lower case here marks the distinction in the psalm.

notes.phrase: two tiny copper coins, which make a penny
notes.traditional: two mites, which make a farthing
notes.note: The Greek names two lepta, the smallest coins in circulation in Judea, and explains their value as one quadrans, the smallest Roman coin, worth one sixty-fourth of a denarius. The explanation in Roman terms is often taken as a hint about the audience Mark wrote for. “Penny” stands for the lowest coin in use and is not an exact equivalent.
